SimQueueBase shares built-in coordination but intentionally does not expose external storage hooks; private protected construction protects transactional permit accounting.
Count reports physical FIFO occupancy, including values reserved for a pending consumer. Tested during immediate operations and reserved handoffs.
Capacity is immutable and strictly positive, default int.MaxValue; nonpositive sizes do not mean unbounded as in Python.
IsEmpty describes physical occupancy, not whether another caller may consume a reserved item. Handoff tests distinguish these states.
IsFull reports Count == Capacity with positive finite capacity; there is no Python nonpositive-unbounded mode. A free physical slot may be reserved.
Put uses FIFO reserved slots and cancellable semaphore acquisition rather than wake-and-recheck occupancy. Tests cover blocked producers, cancellation before handoff cleanup and pre-cancelled tokens.
TryPut is immediate and boolean; it refuses to steal slots reserved for queued producers even if the physical queue is not full.

Get transfers oldest FIFO items using reserved item permits. Cancellation returns granted-but-unconsumed permits to surviving waiters; unlike Python occupancy loops, newcomers cannot steal a reservation.
TryGet returns boolean/out value and refuses to steal reserved items even if Count is positive; tests verify null payloads and default on failure.

The pinned completed-outcome abstraction has Value/Error subclasses. C# uses Task/Task<T> completion state and SimJob wrappers; no public Outcome class or Python outcome protocol is provided. Pending and cancelled tasks are separate .NET states, not additional Python Outcome variants.

Upstream abstract get is implemented by completed value/error wrappers. C# typed Result explicitly rejects unfinished jobs instead of blocking the simulator, and awaits propagate completion/failure/cancellation. This is a stateful job contract rather than a callable completed Outcome interface.

Pinned Error stores a Python BaseException. C# faults Task<T> and exposes AggregateException through Task.Exception while await/GetAwaiter.GetResult rethrows the underlying .NET exception. Python traceback manipulation and BaseException taxonomy are outside this mapping.

Pinned Error.get raises its stored exception. C# GetAwaiter.GetResult on a faulted job throws the original FormatException; existing completion/introspection regressions check the original error and managed stack. Exception-class identity across Python and .NET is not claimed.

reviews.reason: Pinned TestSuite wraps an Element with mutable tests/failure/error/skip/time counters. C# derives a single suite snapshot from completed TestResult rows; it has no public mutable suite handle or multi-class suite cache. Only report generation is mapped, not construction or Python Element protocols.

Pinned update writes five mutable counters and rounds suite time to three decimals. C# derives tests/failures/skipped from the final rows and writes each case wall duration as an invariant XML number. No separately callable update, error-status counter or rounded aggregate suite-time contract is provided.

Pinned XUnitReporter is an application-constructible accumulating reporter with per-class suites, default attachments and path normalization. SharpTestBench regression owns final result publication through an internal JUnit builder. This internal mapping does not provide the upstream configurable reporter API.

Pinned add_testcase handles passed/failed/skipped/error/xfailed and arbitrary properties, output streams and attachments. C# derives passed/failed/skipped testcase elements from TestResult; expected exceptions become passed and errors remain failure payloads. XML-illegal UTF-16 is visibly escaped while JSON keeps original text. Attachment/property and Python traceback protocols remain outside this mapping.

Pinned write updates counters, creates parents and saves UTF-8 XML. C# regression writes discovery/results/functional JSON and JUnit beside the configured results path. Successful XML serialization is covered separately from simulator shutdown; atomic multi-file publication and artifact I/O failure shutdown are not established by this mapping.

Pinned normalize_path caches path objects and optionally makes resolved paths relative to a configured root. C# leaves application exception paths intact in JSON and XML text; it has no mutable reporter base path or attachment cache. Automatic relative-path rewriting is intentionally absent to preserve original diagnostic evidence.
Python coroutine protocol base maps to C# awaitable Trigger/Task infrastructure. No exported Python _wait or await-protocol identity is reproduced.

C# trigger Combine owns subscriptions; SimTasks.Combine borrows tasks and waits all even after fault/cancellation. Upstream deprecated task inputs and FIRST_EXCEPTION cancellation differ; no exact semantic parity claim.

C# SimTasks.First returns winning Task and leaves losers caller-owned, including external cancellation. Trigger First returns its trigger identity; mixed upstream coroutine result semantics are separate.

One-bit C# cycle wait supports rising/falling/any through explicit ClockEdge, preserves original cancellation overload, validates zero count and rejects negative count. Returns Task rather than an inspectable Python Waitable.
Clock operand is supplied to the C# asynchronous method; returned Task has no reverse signal property. Operand ownership/width is validated even for zero cycles.
Count is an explicit C# method argument, not stored on an inspectable Waitable. Negative counts reject and zero validates without callbacks.
C# exposes ClockEdge enum as a required fourth argument, not a Python trigger class stored on a returned Waitable. Original rising-only overload remains source-compatible.
C# uses System.TimeoutException for simulation deadlines, not a dedicated cocotb exception class. Classification is shared with other managed timeout sources.

Borrowed C# tasks survive deadline expiry; typed values and original faults propagate and the internal timer is joined. Owned deferred operations use explicit ownership APIs, and completed-task ties win; Python select result/coroutine policy differs.
SimJob wraps scheduled C# delegates/.NET Task rather than a Python coroutine/state-machine object; construction, introspection and exception surfaces differ.
SimTaskLocal<T> uses typed identity keys, distinguishes missing/null and isolates nested jobs; Python arbitrary attribute namespaces are not copied.
SimJob.Name exposes the diagnostic name; automatic names are assigned per test job registration. Initial blank names reject without reserving an ordinal.
SetName takes a nonblank string on the simulator thread; upstream stringifies arbitrary objects and accepts empty strings.
Abrupt Python coroutine kill/result=None has no managed counterpart; cooperative Cancel deliberately runs C# cleanup. Do not treat cancellation as abrupt-kill parity.
SimJob.Complete waits terminal state without propagating the result, fault or cancellation; the original Task retains its outcome. Its await result is void rather than a Python TaskComplete object.
Deprecated Python join wrapper is omitted; await SimJob/SimJob<T> propagates completion/result directly.

Cancel requests cooperative cancellation using the job token, returns void and accepts no message; completed results are not rewritten. Python cancellation request/suppression and return-value semantics differ.
Task.IsCanceled exposes .NET terminal cancellation after joining. An uncancelled OperationCanceledException can fault a managed job; Python CancelledError state rules are not copied.
IsCompleted/Task.IsCompleted reports all terminal .NET task states, including success and cancellation, without blocking.
Typed Result returns/throws the original terminal outcome; unfinished access rejects synchronously instead of blocking, using managed exception types.
SimJob.Exception uses .NET Task.Exception: AggregateException on fault and null for unfinished/success/cancelled; upstream throws for unfinished/cancelled and returns the original fault.
SimJob.Current identifies StartSoon async flow and is null in the test body; upstream raises when no task runs. Nested continuation identity is preserved.
The completion-only concept is exposed as a reusable Trigger rather than a public Python TaskComplete class/protocol. It does not propagate a job outcome.
C# callers retain the originating SimJob reference; completion triggers do not publicly expose a reverse task lookup.

reviews.reason: Private Python ANSI colour constants are not a public C# object model. Structured SimulationLog emits typed JSON events; no matching escape-code namespace or colour-format equivalence is claimed.

SimClock is an explicitly owned managed/native-capability driver with simulator-step timing and cycle-boundary updates. Upstream retains requested physical units and value types, chooses its own auto policy and default set action, and rejects an odd default half-period; C# deliberately permits unequal integer halves. No constructor/default-policy equivalence is claimed.

Signal returns the same driven C# Signal instance after an owner-thread check. Upstream returns its LogicObject without reproducing the managed ownership guard or wrapper type; matching driven-handle intent does not imply wrapper identity across languages.

PeriodSteps reports configured integer simulator steps, including the next-cycle pending setting. Python period retains the original numeric value in its requested unit; this is not a dimensionally identical property or a statement about the pulse currently in flight.

HighSteps is the configured next-cycle integer high duration. Upstream period_high retains requested-unit numeric form; C# updates preserve the current whole pulse pair. No current-pulse timing or numeric-type equivalence is claimed.

SimClock accepts simulator-step counts and exposes PeriodSteps/HighSteps/LowSteps, with no retained physical-unit property. Runtime.Steps performs an explicit positive decimal conversion; physical-unit preservation is not implemented by the clock.

Implementation reports the requested Auto/Managed/Native policy. Upstream impl reports its resolved py/gpi implementation; Auto in this C# property must not be used to infer which backend actually drives a run.

Upstream exposes the selected Immediate/Deposit/Force clock action. SimClock has no set-action constructor/property and its managed loop uses the default WriteBit deposit. General Signal write actions are not evidence that configurable clock actions are implemented.

Upstream start schedules and retains its own task and defaults to an initial high pulse. C# Run is a caller-owned Task using cooperative cancellation and initially drives low. Duplicate ownership is rejected, but initial phase, scheduling and returned-task lifecycle are not exact equivalents.

Upstream stop requests cancellation and immediately drops its stored task, permitting restart without joining. C# callers cancel and join the run; ownership remains held through cleanup. There is no Clock.stop method or equivalent unjoined restart guarantee.

C# ClockCycles counts subscribed selected transitions and validates zero-count operands/ownership. Python Clock.cycles synchronizes on an edge and may substitute timers derived from its configured period. External/changing clocks, zero counts and timer optimizations are not interchangeable.

HdlObject owns a native handle and enforces simulator-thread access. Child/index caches preserve selected wrapper identities, but repeated Root/conversion calls are not a global native-handle identity/equality cache like the Python handle factory/base protocol.

Python exposes AUTO versus NATIVE lookup discovery. C# has status-bearing discovery queries but no public per-lookup native-only/automatic selection argument. Successful observations do not establish complete mixed-language discovery.

C# uses Child/Children/Walk rather than Python attribute and dict-like discovery. Missing named children raise KeyNotFoundException; backend names and cached child wrappers are supported, but Python attribute rules and hierarchy mapping interfaces are not copied.

HdlArray<T> binds children by declared HDL indices and enumerates in Range order. Explicit converters, checked offset/index exceptions and backend range availability differ from the Python hierarchy-array factory/protocol.

WriteAction.Deposit queues a checked C# write; last deferred writes can coalesce before a ReadWrite flush. Python Deposit is a typed action object dispatched through generic value setters. Matching deposition intent does not establish arbitrary backend delta or action-object protocol parity.

C# exposes WriteAction.Force and typed force helpers with thread/phase/constant/capability guards. There is no generic Python Force action object, and supported force/release behavior is qualified per backend, not universally across HDL types.

Upstream Freeze captures an object current value and forces it through generic action dispatch. C# exposes force/release but no generic Freeze action or equivalent operation. A manually composed read-then-force is not implementation evidence for this API.

Signal.Release requests the checked Release write action with a dummy packed payload. Python Release is a generic action supporting value-object dispatch. Driver recomputation and retained register values remain backend-specific; no generic all-type release equivalence is claimed.

WriteAction.Immediate applies a guarded C# write without deferred deposit scheduling. This is the immediate-write concept, not a Python generic Immediate wrapper or a promise of identical VHDL/Verilog delta ordering on unqualified backends.

C# separates typed Signal, IntegerSignal, RealSignal and StringSignal wrappers under HdlObject rather than a generic value-bearing Python base. Conversions and write actions are explicit; generic action/assignment coercion and factory behavior are not reproduced.
Python value getter forwards to the per-type get implementation. C# requires explicit typed reads and has no universal value property, dynamic return factory or wrapper identity guarantee.

Python value setter rejects ReadOnly/constants then dispatches generic action wrappers or a default deposit. C# typed writes use runtime guards and explicit actions, without the full assignment union or Freeze dispatcher.

The abstract Python get contract is implemented by per-type wrappers. C# uses explicit Read/ReadBits/ReadUInt/ReadSInt methods with typed returns and thread guards; there is no universal generic value-get method.

C# typed Write methods and WriteAction implement selected mutations with runtime validation. They do not accept the entire Python action/value union, arbitrary assignment conversions or a generic Freeze action.

The deprecated Python setter rewrites deposits/unwrapped values to a legacy immediate action before value dispatch. C# omits that alias; WriteAction.Immediate is explicit and does not claim the alias historical timing/coercion semantics.

HdlObject.IsConstant queries the same native GPI constant metadata on the owning thread. Writes separately reject constants. This is the constness-query concept only, not generic wrapper/factory equality or metadata support on every backend.

HdlArray<T> is a typed cached child binding with declared HDL range, not a generic Python array value object. ValueArray<T> is separate managed value storage; child wrappers versus aggregate values and assignment operations remain distinct.

C# callers explicitly enumerate typed HdlArray bindings and read chosen leaf types; there is no generic aggregate live-handle get returning Python Array values. Range-aware ValueArray storage is an explicit alternative, not evidence of automatic aggregate snapshot equivalence.

Python writes aggregate arrays element-by-element in positional order with generic actions. HdlArray<T> exposes bindings through IReadOnlyCollection and no aggregate write/action operation. Manually looping over leaves does not implement this setter contract.

C# scalar signals use Signal/Signal<W1>, strict bool conversion or LogicArray readback rather than a dynamically selected Python LogicObject with generic value assignment. State preservation and allowed writes remain capability-qualified.

ReadBit returns a strict bool conversion while ReadLogic preserves logic text/range. Neither is the Python Logic return type; unresolved/weak-state conversion and exception types require explicit C# choices.

C# offers bool WriteBit and checked-width WriteBits/typed writes with explicit actions. It does not reproduce the entire Python int/string/Logic/LogicArray assignment coercion union, action objects or exception classes.

Triggers.RisingEdge creates a new checked one-bit trigger. Python exposes a cached handle property that rejects constants before returning its edge trigger. C# factory identity and constant-edge preflight are not declared equivalent.

Triggers.FallingEdge creates an independently subscribed one-bit trigger. Python cached property identity and immutable-handle rejection are separate behavior; C# transition tests do not establish property/factory parity for constants or every backend transition.

C# packed transport and explicit PackedStruct/PackedArray views use checked schemas and available bit ranges. Python dynamically exposes packed handles/bit children. Explicit schemas do not establish automatic field inference or packed metadata beyond qualified backends.

C# Signal<W>/LogicSignal<W> provide explicit fixed-width/range-aware values with capability checks. Python dynamically maps HDL logic arrays and indexes child LogicObjects. Type factories, width limits, indexed-object behavior and numeric coercion are not identical.

RealSignal explicitly validates native kind and uses double read/write APIs. Python real objects participate in generic value/action assignment and accept float/int conversion. Matching native floating transport does not establish the generic object protocol or backend availability.

RealSignal.Read obtains the native floating getter as C# double on the simulator thread, corresponding narrowly to the Python float read concept. This does not certify real-object discovery, unusual values or all backend floating semantics.

RealSignal.Write accepts double plus explicit WriteAction and runtime guards. Python dispatches its float/int/action union. There is no generic Freeze action, Python conversion protocol or universal real-force capability claim.

IntegerSignal exposes raw native enums, while EnumSignal<T> requires explicit defined C# numeric members. Upstream returns integer representations with width/signedness correction and does not infer declaration names. These mapping and validation policies differ.

Raw IntegerSignal.Read returns the native long without upstream width/signedness correction or wide binary fallback. EnumSignal<T> additionally rejects unmapped values. Neither establishes the full Python enum integer-get domain.

EnumSignal<T>.Write requires a defined C# member and checked int32 conversion. Python accepts any fitting integer representation without named-member validation, including wider underlying values. Raw IntegerSignal.Write is an int32 alternative, not full enum assignment parity.

The native IntegerSignal wrapper reads native long and writes int32. Upstream determines declared width/signedness, adjusts reads and uses binary transport for wide writes. Explicit fixed-width packed APIs are alternatives only on suitable objects, not completion of the native integer contract.

IntegerSignal.Read does not perform narrow sign-extension correction, unsigned negative normalization or the greater-than-32-bit binary fallback present upstream. Platform native-long behavior must not be reported as portable declared-integer equivalence.

IntegerSignal.Write accepts int32 and delegates to GPI, rather than validating against every declared width/signedness and supporting wider binary values as upstream does. Runtime phase/constant checks do not fill those numeric-domain gaps.

StringSignal uses Latin-1 C# string and explicit kind/phase/capability guards, while Python uses bytes/bytearray. Fixed and dynamic reads differ, and dynamic embedded NUL is not an arbitrary byte-string round-trip guarantee.

C# reads fixed strings by declared length and dynamic strings by scanning to terminating NUL, then decodes Latin-1. Python returns native bytes. Encoding, return type and dynamic NUL limitations prevent generic byte-for-byte equivalence.

C# rejects non-Latin-1 characters, requires exact fixed length and uses checked character handles for NUL. Python accepts bytes/bytearray and generic actions. Native padding/truncation descriptions are not a promise that C# reproduces arbitrary byte assignments.

Upstream fixed-string override rejects oversized byte values but permits shorter values for native padding; C# requires exact fixed length. Fixed-length NUL transport is supported through checked character handles, without reproducing Python bytes/action or short-value padding behavior.
